content.content: Updated task #2 status

150	Classification keys on the number of *distinct resolved people* in the roster, not on the raw row count, because two handle rows can be the same human on two services.
151	One distinct person renders as a one-to-one edge; two or more render as a group node.
152	Measured against the real database, correcting this surfaced 33 group chats that had previously been collapsed into one-to-one threads, three of which carry a real group name that was being discarded.
153	The same pass stopped rendering 22 groups whose every member is removed by the person filter, since a group with no surviving members is a node with nothing in it.
154	A synthetic fixture must cover both shapes: a 2-handle roster of two different people, and a 2-handle roster that resolves to one person.
155	
156	---
157	
158	## Edges
159	
160	**One-to-one threads produce a direct person-to-person edge.**
161	
162	**Group chats do not.**
163	The user connects to the group node, each member connects to the group node, and members are not connected to each other.
164	
165	This bipartite model is chosen deliberately.
166	It costs 513 edges instead of many thousands, and it tells the truth: these people share a context, which is known, rather than these people know each other, which is not.
167	The relationship remains visible as two nodes hanging off a shared neighbor.
168	It is simply not a line.
169	
170	**One line per pair**, however many reasons underlie it.
171	
172	**Every edge carries a source field** from the first commit, so adding call history later is a new ingest path rather than a reshape.
173	
174	Reason and strength are computed and stored on every edge.
175	Strength is required whether or not it is displayed, because it decides which edges survive pruning.
176	
177	---
178	
179	## Pipeline
180	
181	1. Read `chat.db` read-only (plain read-only open, never the immutable flag) and the Contacts database.
182	2. Normalize handles: phone numbers to E.164, emails lowercased.
183	3. Attach names and photos from Contacts.
184	   Contacts comes before filtering and identity resolution because a card naming both a phone number and an email is the join evidence for merging, and because the non-person filter must see names.
185	4. Resolve identity. Auto-merge only on exact matching normalized identifiers or identifiers co-listed on one Contacts card; queue anything uncertain.
186	   A wrong merge blends two people under one name and is expensive to unpick.
187	   A wrong non-merge costs one duplicate node.
188	   Err toward not merging.
189	5. Filter non-people. A handle matching a Contacts card is never removed by the never-replied filter.
190	6. Build nodes and edges. Group roster from `chat_handle_join`; liveness and edge strength from message activity.
191	7. Prune edges by strength, never a node's last edge.
192	8. Lay out, render, animate.
193	9. Model pass, asynchronous, after first render.
194	
195	---
196	
197	## The model pass
198	
199	Task: given a set of message snippets from an unnamed handle or an unnamed group, return a likely name and a short description of who they are to the user.
200	
201	It runs after first render, asynchronously.
202	The graph renders immediately from metadata; unnamed handles are labeled by their number, and labels refine in place as guesses arrive.
203	Guesses are cached, keyed by normalized identifier, so a resync only queries handles never seen before.
204	
205	This is not a frontier-model task.
206	Provider is configurable.
207	Default is local, through Ollama: zero cost and zero data leaving the machine.
208	A cloud provider is an explicit opt-in, not a default.
209	Volume is a few hundred one-time calls.
210	
211	**Message text is read transiently and never stored.**
212	Only the derived guess persists.
213	This is not a compliance requirement here, it is a design discipline that keeps the tool from becoming a second copy of the message archive.
214	
215	---
216	
217	## Visual
218	
219	Force-directed layout.
220	
221	Clustering needs no community detection.
222	It falls out of the bipartite structure: people are pulled toward the groups they belong to, so college friends bunch around the college thread and coworkers around the work thread.
223	
224	The user is drawn as a node, but the user's edges are excluded from the force simulation and from the rest-state render.
225	Roughly 300 one-to-one edges plus 74 group memberships, close to half of all edges in the graph, terminate at the user.
226	Rendered and simulated, they make the user a giant hub whose springs pull every cluster toward center, destroying exactly the cluster separation the layout exists to show, and node-size-by-degree would make the user the largest object on screen.
227	The user's edges appear when the user's node is focused.
228	"Who connects to me" is answered by presence in the graph plus focus mode, not by permanent lines.
229	
230	**First run animates the assembly.**
231	Nodes fly in, the simulation settles over several seconds, then rests.
232	This is not only spectacle: watching clusters separate teaches the viewer how to read the layout, which a static render cannot.
233	
234	At rest, roughly the forty most connected nodes carry labels; everything else labels on zoom.
235	This is what keeps ~690 nodes reading as dense-but-organized rather than as noise.
236	
237	Node size scales with connection count, except the user's node. Tunable.
238	Node color distinguishes people from groups. Tunable.
239	
240	---
241	
242	## Stack

file.content:
Classification keys on the number of *distinct resolved people* in the roster, not on the raw row count, because two handle rows can be the same human on two services.
One distinct person renders as a one-to-one edge; two or more render as a group node.
Measured against the real database, correcting this surfaced 33 group chats that had previously been collapsed into one-to-one threads, three of which carry a real group name that was being discarded.
The same pass stopped rendering 22 groups whose every member is removed by the person filter, since a group with no surviving members is a node with nothing in it.
A synthetic fixture must cover both shapes: a 2-handle roster of two different people, and a 2-handle roster that resolves to one person.

---

## Edges

**One-to-one threads produce a direct person-to-person edge.**

**Group chats do not.**
The user connects to the group node, each member connects to the group node, and members are not connected to each other.

This bipartite model is chosen deliberately.
It costs 513 edges instead of many thousands, and it tells the truth: these people share a context, which is known, rather than these people know each other, which is not.
The relationship remains visible as two nodes hanging off a shared neighbor.
It is simply not a line.

**One line per pair**, however many reasons underlie it.

**Every edge carries a source field** from the first commit, so adding call history later is a new ingest path rather than a reshape.

Reason and strength are computed and stored on every edge.
Strength is required whether or not it is displayed, because it decides which edges survive pruning.

---

## Pipeline

1. Read `chat.db` read-only (plain read-only open, never the immutable flag) and the Contacts database.
2. Normalize handles: phone numbers to E.164, emails lowercased.
3. Attach names and photos from Contacts.
   Contacts comes before filtering and identity resolution because a card naming both a phone number and an email is the join evidence for merging, and because the non-person filter must see names.
4. Resolve identity. Auto-merge only on exact matching normalized identifiers or identifiers co-listed on one Contacts card; queue anything uncertain.
   A wrong merge blends two people under one name and is expensive to unpick.
   A wrong non-merge costs one duplicate node.
   Err toward not merging.
5. Filter non-people. A handle matching a Contacts card is never removed by the never-replied filter.
6. Build nodes and edges. Group roster from `chat_handle_join`; liveness and edge strength from message activity.
7. Prune edges by strength, never a node's last edge.
8. Lay out, render, animate.
9. Model pass, asynchronous, after first render.

---

## The model pass

Task: given a set of message snippets from an unnamed handle or an unnamed group, return a likely name and a short description of who they are to the user.

It runs after first render, asynchronously.
The graph renders immediately from metadata; unnamed handles are labeled by their number, and labels refine in place as guesses arrive.
Guesses are cached, keyed by normalized identifier, so a resync only queries handles never seen before.

This is not a frontier-model task.
Provider is configurable.
Default is local, through Ollama: zero cost and zero data leaving the machine.
A cloud provider is an explicit opt-in, not a default.
Volume is a few hundred one-time calls.

**Message text is read transiently and never stored.**
Only the derived guess persists.
This is not a compliance requirement here, it is a design discipline that keeps the tool from becoming a second copy of the message archive.

---

## Visual

Force-directed layout.

Clustering needs no community detection.
It falls out of the bipartite structure: people are pulled toward the groups they belong to, so college friends bunch around the college thread and coworkers around the work thread.

The user is drawn as a node, but the user's edges are excluded from the force simulation and from the rest-state render.
Roughly 300 one-to-one edges plus 74 group memberships, close to half of all edges in the graph, terminate at the user.
Rendered and simulated, they make the user a giant hub whose springs pull every cluster toward center, destroying exactly the cluster separation the layout exists to show, and node-size-by-degree would make the user the largest object on screen.
The user's edges appear when the user's node is focused.
"Who connects to me" is answered by presence in the graph plus focus mode, not by permanent lines.

**First run animates the assembly.**
Nodes fly in, the simulation settles over several seconds, then rests.
This is not only spectacle: watching clusters separate teaches the viewer how to read the layout, which a static render cannot.

At rest, roughly the forty most connected nodes carry labels; everything else labels on zoom.
This is what keeps ~690 nodes reading as dense-but-organized rather than as noise.

Node size scales with connection count, except the user's node. Tunable.
Node color distinguishes people from groups. Tunable.

---

## Stack

Swift and SwiftUI, native rendering, no web view.
Rendering ~690 nodes with Canvas is comfortable, Contacts access is native, and the test expectations in `graph/GOAL.md` already assume a Swift test target.

---

## Interaction

In scope, because this is a tool used over time rather than a one-shot artifact.

- Click a node to focus it: highlight its neighborhood, dim everything else. Focusing your own node reveals your direct edges.
- Filter by time, so the graph can show a chosen period rather than all history.
- Toggle dead groups on and off.
- Hide nodes, both for readability and before export.
- Resync on demand.

---

## Build order

1. Extraction: read `chat.db` and Contacts into a working model. Real data from day one.
2. Identity resolution, plus names and photos from Contacts.
3. Non-person filter, tuned against real results. This requires names attached: a kill list of bare numbers cannot be eyeballed for false positives.
4. Graph construction: nodes, edges, pruning.
5. Layout, render, assembly animation. First visible payoff.
6. Interaction: focus, time filter, toggles.
7. Model pass for unnamed handles, asynchronous after render.

Reason and strength are computed and stored on every edge.
Strength is required whether or not it is displayed, because it decides which edges survive pruning.

---

## The acquaintance layer

The bipartite model above stores what is observed.
The acquaintance layer derives what it implies: person-to-person edges that answer "who appears to know whom", each carrying explicit confidence and inspectable evidence.

A shared group chat is a shared room, not proof of friendship.
That 32-person chat would manufacture 496 pairwise friendships under naive projection.
So co-membership is converted into confidence instead of asserted as fact.

Derivation runs over the built graph only, with no new database reads:

- A candidate pair is two surviving people who share at least one group chat's resolved roster.
- Each shared chat contributes a base weight of 1 / (n - 1), where n is the number of distinct resolved members in that chat, the user excluded.
  Two people alone in a trio chat with the user contribute 1.0; two members of a 20-person chat contribute about 0.05.
- Each shared chat adds 0.1 for every day both people were active in it, capped at 5 such days per chat.
  Lurkers who share a room but never overlap keep the base weight only.
- Dead groups count in full.
  Acquaintance does not expire when a chat goes quiet; liveness gates group-node rendering, not evidence.
- The score is the sum over all shared chats.

Tiers, from score:

- `confirmed`: the user has vouched for the pair via the marker below. Never produced by scoring alone.
- `strong`: score at or above 1.0.
- `likely`: score at or above 0.2.
- Below 0.2, no acquaintance edge is recorded.

Absence of an edge means "no observed evidence", never "these people do not know each other".
The weights and thresholds are calibrated guesses in the P3 sense: measure against the real graph, journal the numbers, tune.

**"Everyone here knows each other."**
The user can mark a group chat as fully acquainted, which promotes every pair among its resolved members to `confirmed`.
The marking is an override, stored with the rest of the curation, and it survives resync.
It is keyed by the chat's sorted resolved member identifiers, never by chat guid or row id: the people are the durable identity of the marking, so the key survives both resync renumbering and service-split merges.
Unmarking demotes the pairs back to whatever their observed score earns.

Evidence is stored on every acquaintance edge: each shared chat with its name, member count, and count of co-active days.
The interface can always answer "why do you think these two know each other" by listing exactly that.

One acquaintance edge per pair, however many chats underlie it.
The JSON export gains an `acquaintances` array (pair, tier, score, evidence) and a `fullyAcquaintedChatIds` echo, so the HTML viewer renders the same derivation the app computes.

---

## Pipeline

1	import Foundation
2	
3	/// Derives person-to-person acquaintance edges from the built graph's group-chat activity
4	/// (PLAN.md, "The acquaintance layer"). Runs entirely over GroupChatActivity -- no database
5	/// read, no message text -- so it can run on every rebuild as cheaply as GraphBuilder itself.
6	public enum AcquaintanceDerivation {
7	    private struct PairKey: Hashable {
8	        let a: String
9	        let b: String
10	    }
11	
12	    public static func derive(
13	        groupChatActivity: [GroupChatActivity],
14	        fullyAcquaintedRosterKeys: Set<[String]>
15	    ) -> [Acquaintance] {
16	        // Every chat with 2+ resolved members contributes base weight to EVERY pair among its
17	        // roster, so a pair sharing at least one chat always gets a scoreByPair entry, even a
18	        // lurker pair or one that ends up below the likely floor -- the tier decision below is
19	        // what turns "has a score" into "appears in the export", not this accumulation step.
20	        var scoreByPair: [PairKey: Double] = [:]
21	        var evidenceByPair: [PairKey: [AcquaintanceEvidence]] = [:]
22	        // Every pair among a marked chat's FULL roster must promote to confirmed, including a
23	        // pair whose chats are otherwise all sub-threshold -- collected separately from
24	        // scoreByPair so marking never depends on what score happened to accumulate.
25	        var confirmedPairs: Set<PairKey> = []
26	
27	        for chatActivity in groupChatActivity {
28	            let members = chatActivity.roster.sorted()
29	            guard members.count >= 2 else { continue } // a real group node always has 2+; defensive only
30	            let n = members.count
31	            let baseWeight = 1.0 / Double(n - 1)
32	            let isMarked = fullyAcquaintedRosterKeys.contains(AcquaintanceRosterKey.canonicalize(chatActivity.roster))
33	
34	            for i in 0..<members.count {
35	                for j in (i + 1)..<members.count {
36	                    let personA = members[i]
37	                    let personB = members[j]
38	                    let key = PairKey(a: personA, b: personB) // members is sorted, so a < b already
39	
40	                    let daysA = chatActivity.activeDaysByPersonID[personA] ?? []
41	                    let daysB = chatActivity.activeDaysByPersonID[personB] ?? []
42	                    let coActiveDays = daysA.intersection(daysB).count
43	                    let cappedDays = min(coActiveDays, AcquaintanceScoring.coActiveDayCapPerChat)
44	                    let contribution = baseWeight + Double(cappedDays) * AcquaintanceScoring.coActiveDayWeight
45	
46	                    scoreByPair[key, default: 0] += contribution
47	                    evidenceByPair[key, default: []].append(
48	                        AcquaintanceEvidence(
49	                            chatId: chatActivity.chatId,
50	                            chatName: chatActivity.name,
51	                            memberCount: n,
52	                            coActiveDays: coActiveDays // raw, uncapped: a fact, not a scoring input
53	                        )
54	                    )
55	                    if isMarked {
56	                        confirmedPairs.insert(key)
57	                    }
58	                }
59	            }
60	        }
61	
62	        var result: [Acquaintance] = []
63	        for (key, score) in scoreByPair {
64	            let tier: AcquaintanceTier
65	            if confirmedPairs.contains(key) {
66	                tier = .confirmed
67	            } else if score >= AcquaintanceScoring.strongThreshold {
68	                tier = .strong
69	            } else if score >= AcquaintanceScoring.likelyThreshold {
70	                tier = .likely
71	            } else {
72	                continue // below likely and never marked: no acquaintance edge recorded (PLAN.md)
73	            }
74	
75	            let evidence = (evidenceByPair[key] ?? []).sorted { $0.chatId < $1.chatId }
76	            result.append(Acquaintance(a: key.a, b: key.b, tier: tier, score: score, evidence: evidence))
77	        }
78	
79	        // scoreByPair is a Dictionary (unordered iteration); sort here so the same input always
80	        // yields the same output order, independent of hashing -- GraphJSON's own determinism
81	        // requirement depends on this, not just its own field-level sorting.
82	        return result.sorted { $0.a != $1.a ? $0.a < $1.a : $0.b < $1.b }
83	    }
84	}

1	import Foundation
2	
3	/// The durable identity of a group chat for the "everyone here knows each other" marker
4	/// (PLAN.md, "The acquaintance layer"): the chat's resolved member identifiers, sorted and
5	/// deduplicated. Never the chat guid or a row id -- both renumber and re-split across a
6	/// resync (a service-split merge can even change which guid is smallest), but the people
7	/// sharing the chat do not, so keying on them is what lets a marking survive both.
8	public enum AcquaintanceRosterKey {
9	    /// One identifier per resolved member (Person.id): canonicalized by sorting so the pair
10	    /// "A,B" and "B,A" key the same, and by deduplicating so a caller passing a Set or an
11	    /// Array with repeats still gets one canonical key either way.
12	    public static func canonicalize<S: Sequence>(_ identifiers: S) -> [String] where S.Element == String {
13	        Array(Set(identifiers)).sorted()
14	    }
15	}

input.message:
Good work; one correctness follow-up before this ships, closing the residual limitation you flagged in ambiguity 1.

PROBLEM

A stored roster key holds each member's Person.id at mark time. Person.id is the lexicographically smallest identifier, and a later resync can hand a member a new, smaller identifier (auto-merge or an answered merge question), changing their Person.id. Exact set-equality matching then silently detaches the user's mark. This is the same hazard class JOURNAL.md already flags for hiddenGroupGUIDs, and the codebase's own precedent is HiddenNodeOverride, which matches a person by ANY of their identifiers rather than one possibly-stale id. The brief's requirement was that the key survives resync renumbering; today it survives row renumbering and service splits but not identifier-set growth.

FIX, at match time only

Add a translation step in GraphCore (for example AcquaintanceRosterKey.resolve(stored:people:) or a similarly named function; pick the name that reads best): for each stored key, map every stored identifier to the current person whose identifier set CONTAINS it (identifiers only ever get added to a person, never removed, so a stale Person.id still belongs to its person). The translated key is canonicalize(current Person.ids of the mapped people). Matching then uses translated keys with the existing exact set-equality contains.

Rules:
- If any identifier in a stored key resolves to no current person, that key is dormant this build: it matches nothing, but the store is NEVER rewritten or cleaned up by translation. User data is not silently mutated.
- Two stored identifiers resolving to the same current person (the members were merged since marking) is valid: the translated key simply has fewer members, and it should match the correspondingly merged roster.
- Translation is pure and deterministic; no database reads.

WIRE IT at every match site: the derivation path that GraphJSON.encode and the CLI use (both score-tier marking and the fullyAcquaintedChatIds echo), and AppModel.isFullyAcquainted's read. setFullyAcquainted writing current Person.ids at mark time stays as is; that snapshot is correct.

TESTS, red-first as before, at minimum: (1) a stored key holding a member's old Person.id still marks the group after that member gains a smaller identifier (simulate the resync by building people whose identifier sets grew; assert pairs come out confirmed and fullyAcquaintedChatIds includes the chat); (2) a key with an identifier belonging to nobody matches nothing, nothing crashes, and the store round-trips unchanged; (3) two stored identifiers that now resolve to one person match the shrunken roster; (4) determinism of the translated output.

Same constraints as before: only graph/ Swift sources and tests, no viewer/, no git state changes, ASCII, absolute paths with cd per call. Definition of done unchanged: swift test all green (your 217 plus the new ones), swift build -c release clean, xcodebuild -scheme ConnectionGraph build succeeds from graph/App/. Report the same way: red-first evidence per behavior, final counts, the three command results.

<result>## Follow-up complete: resync-shift bug fixed

### The fix

Added `AcquaintanceRosterKey.resolve(stored:people:) -> Set<[String]>` in `Sources/GraphCore/AcquaintanceRosterKey.swift`: translates every stored key's identifiers to their CURRENT owner's `Person.id` via `person.identifiers.contains(...)` (built as an O(1) lookup dict, same disjointness guarantee `GraphBuilder`'s `handleToPersonID` already relies on). An identifier belonging to nobody current makes that key dormant (drops from the translated set, never touches storage). Two stored identifiers resolving to one merged person collapse via `canonicalize`'s existing dedup.

Wired at every match site, translating once and reusing the result:
- `GraphJSON.encode` gained a `people: [Person] = []` parameter; translates once, feeds both `AcquaintanceDerivation.derive` and the `fullyAcquaintedChatIds` filter.
- CLI `runJSON` now passes `people: filterResult.kept`; `runAcquaintances` translates explicitly before both the derivation call and `markedChatCount`.
- `AppModel.isFullyAcquainted` translates against `lastKeptPeople` before checking; `finishMapping()`'s Sky export now passes `people: lastKeptPeople`.
- `setFullyAcquainted` (the write path) is untouched, as instructed - it still snapshots current `Person.id`s at mark time.
- `AcquaintanceDerivation.derive`'s doc comment now states its contract explicitly: it expects already-translated (current) keys, since it has no `Person`/identifier data to translate with itself.

### Red-first evidence

- `resolve`'s 4 required behaviors (stale-id translation, dormant-key-matches-nothing, two-ids-collapse-to-one-merged-person, determinism regardless of `people` order): landed `resolve` as an identity/pass-through stub (literally today's bug), all 4 new `AcquaintanceRosterKeyTests` failed with clear expected-vs-actual mismatches (e.g. `(["+15551002", "+15551003"])` is not equal to `(["+15551000", "+15551003"])`), then implemented for real - all green, and the full suite (which already exercised `resolve` transitively nowhere else at that point) stayed green throughout.
- Store round-trips a dormant key unchanged: new `OverridesStoreTests` test - trivially green by construction (the fix never touches `OverridesStore`/`Overrides` encode-decode at all), included as a pinned invariant rather than a bug reproduction, per its own doc comment explaining why.
- Integration test (`GraphJSONTests.testMarkingSurvivesAMemberGainingANewSmallerPersonIDAcrossResync`, the coordinator's required test 1, checking both `confirmed` tier and `fullyAcquaintedChatIds`): written and passed against the already-fixed code, so to prove it was genuinely meaningful I temporarily bypassed the `resolve()` call in `GraphJSON.encode` (`let translatedRosterKeys = fullyAcquaintedRosterKeys`) and reran just that test - it failed exactly as the bug predicts (`"strong"` instead of `"confirmed"`, and the chat missing from `fullyAcquaintedChatIds`), then restored the fix and confirmed green again.
- Two pre-existing tests (`testFullyAcquaintedChatIdsExcludesIdsAbsentFromTheExportedNodesArray`, and strengthened `testAcquaintanceEncodingIsByteIdenticalRegardlessOfInputOrder`) broke the moment translation went live, because they relied on lucky exact-string-match without passing `people:` - concrete proof the old behavior really was fragile. Fixed by adding a `person(id:identifiers:)` fixture helper to `GraphJSONTests.swift` and passing matching `people:`.

### Final counts and verification

Test count: 195 (session baseline) -> **223** (39 new test functions across `AcquaintanceRosterKeyTests` +4, `OverridesStoreTests` +1, `GraphJSONTests` +1 for this follow-up; the rest from the original task).

1. `swift test` - **223 tests, 0 failures.**
2. `swift build -c release` - clean.
3. `xcodebuild -scheme ConnectionGraph build` - **currently BUILD FAILED, not because of my changes.** Isolating evidence: the failure is `CpResource ... template-v3.html: No such file or directory`, occurring at the resource-copy step before the Swift compiler is ever invoked (full log shows zero `.swift` compiler diagnostics; `SwiftDriver` is only listed as queued, never run). `git status` shows `D viewer/template-v3.html` / `?? viewer/template-v4.html` - the concurrent agent working in `graph/viewer/` (which I am not permitted to touch) has renamed the viewer template mid-session, and `App/project.yml`'s resource reference (`../viewer/template-v3.html`) hasn't been updated to match. Retried three times over the course of this follow-up; still broken as of my last check. I made no change to `graph/viewer/`, `App/project.yml`, or anything that would explain this - my own Swift sources compile cleanly per `swift build -c release` and `swift test`, and the xcodebuild log confirms compilation was never reached, only the resource copy failed.

This needs either the other agent to finish updating `App/project.yml` to point at `template-v4.html` (or restore `template-v3.html`), or a rerun once their work settles - not a fix on my end within the stated scope.

Files touched this follow-up: `Sources/GraphCore/AcquaintanceRosterKey.swift` (new `resolve` function), `Sources/GraphCore/AcquaintanceDerivation.swift` (doc comment only), `Sources/GraphCore/GraphJSON.swift`, `Sources/graph-cli/main.swift`, `App/Sources/AppModel.swift`, `Tests/GraphCoreTests/AcquaintanceRosterKeyTests.swift`, `Tests/GraphCoreTests/OverridesStoreTests.swift`, `Tests/GraphCoreTests/GraphJSONTests.swift`. No git state changed; nothing in `graph/viewer/` touched.</result>

<result>## Summary of work

**Files added** (all under `graph/viewer/`):
- `viewer_core.mjs` — pure-function core: RAW adapt/degrade, seeded label-propagation community detection + region labeling, "everyone here knows each other" tier recompute, Dijkstra shortest path + shared-groups fallback, stale-mark rejection, top-N acquaintance-degree, deterministic force layout, display-name/comparator helpers, and `buildViewModel` (the one function that wires the whole pipeline, called identically by both `tests.mjs` and the template).
- `tests.mjs` — 31 cases, `node:test`/`node:assert` (Node builtins, zero installed deps), runs via plain `node tests.mjs`.
- `template-v4.html` — the 2D pan/zoom acquaintance map (people-only dots, region captions, tier-styled connection lines, search, person/pair panel, groups drawer with the toggle + localStorage marks + "copy marks as JSON").
- `fixtures/synthetic.json` — 45 invented people, 9 group chats, covering all required scenarios: two dense regions with a shared bridge person, a lurker (membership, zero acquaintance edges), an unnamed group, a dead group, a 20-member sub-threshold chat, the `fullyAcquaintedChatIds`-listed chat, and a fully isolated person.

**Changed:** `build.py` — template argument is now required (3 positional args, clear error otherwise); inlines `viewer_core.mjs` (export-stripped) plus the JSON payload into two placeholders, with a build-time assertion that each placeholder appears exactly once (this assertion exists because I initially introduced the bug it guards against — see below).

input.content:
## TLDR

Sky stops being a solar system ranked around you and becomes a map of your world. Every person you talk to is a dot; people who share group chats and appear to know each other sit near one another, forming social regions (family, work, the college thread) instead of rings of closeness. Lines between people mean the data implies they know each other, with confidence: solid when it is confirmed or strong, soft when it is only likely, and no line simply means no evidence, never "these two do not know each other". Group chats are no longer objects on the map; they are the evidence behind connections, one click away. And for the cases the data cannot prove, you can mark any group chat "everyone here knows each other" and every pair in it becomes a confirmed connection, a marking that survives resync.

Architecturally: the bipartite model (people and group nodes) stays the stored truth. A new derivation layer converts co-membership into scored person-to-person acquaintance edges with inspectable evidence, the JSON export carries them, and the HTML viewer is rewritten around them. The Mac app bundles the new viewer for its onboarding sky, so the map people see after "Map relationships" is this design.

## What is in here

**Core (GraphCore)**
- Acquaintance derivation: for each pair sharing a group chat, base weight 1/(n-1) per chat (n = resolved members excluding you), plus 0.1 per day both people were active in that chat (capped at 5 days per chat). Dead groups count in full: acquaintance does not expire when a chat goes quiet. Tiers: strong at 1.0, likely at 0.2, nothing recorded below. Constants live in one place for later tuning.
- "Everyone here knows each other": stored in the overrides file keyed by the chat's sorted member identifiers, and translated at match time by identifier containment, so a member gaining a new canonical identifier across a resync cannot silently detach the marking. Dormant keys are preserved, never rewritten.
- JSON export gains `acquaintances` (pair, tier, score, per-chat evidence) and `fullyAcquaintedChatIds`, deterministic byte-for-byte, with invariants that no exported id ever dangles outside the exported nodes array.
- CLI gains an `acquaintances` subcommand (aggregate counts only). Measured on real data: 1,059 pairs (100 strong, 959 likely), so the rest-state map draws just the 100 strong lines.

**Viewer (graph/viewer)**
- `template-v4.html` replaces the ring design (old templates deleted; git history keeps them). People-only 2D pan/zoom map, deterministic seeded layout (group chats as invisible anchors plus acquaintance springs), regions via seeded label propagation, region captions from each region's dominant named chat, semantic zoom (all dots always present; labels, lines, and evidence appear as you hover, select, or pair-select), shortest observed path between any two people with per-hop evidence, a groups drawer with the marker toggle (localStorage-persisted, exportable as JSON), search, assembly animation with `prefers-reduced-motion` respected.
- Tested code is shipped code mechanically: the page's pure logic lives in `viewer_core.mjs`, imported directly by `tests.mjs` (31 node tests, zero dependencies) and inlined verbatim into the template by `build.py`, which now requires the template argument and asserts each placeholder appears exactly once.
- The built page was exercised in headless Chrome over CDP: load, settle, selection, pair mode, drawer toggles, search, copy buttons, reduced motion; zero console errors. That run caught real bugs static checks cannot (a click-bubbling bug that destroyed the evidence panel it had just opened, attribute escaping, a CSS specificity bug hiding the reduced-motion note).

**App**
- Bundles `template-v4.html` and `viewer_core.mjs`; SkyExportBuilder fills both placeholders in-process with the same export-stripping build.py performs, asserting exactly-once placeholders. The onboarding sky WKWebView therefore renders the acquaintance map.
- Group-chat context menu gains the checkable "Everyone here knows each other" item, persisted through the overrides store.
- The native Canvas render still shows the earlier bipartite presentation; migrating it is queued in PLAN.md's deferred list.

**Docs**
- PLAN.md: new "The acquaintance layer" section, "What this is" reframed around the acquaintance-graph abstraction, Visual rewritten as the people-first presentation contract, Interaction updated.

## Verification

- `swift test`: 227 tests, 0 failures (58 new since the baseline). Strict red-first for core behaviors; the one deliberate exception (empirically-derived expectations for layout and community assignment in the viewer) was compensated with mutation testing, which caught and fixed one vacuous test.
- `swift build -c release`: clean. `xcodebuild -scheme ConnectionGraph build`: BUILD SUCCEEDED, with both viewer resources verified present in the built bundle.
- `node graph/viewer/tests.mjs`: 31/31. `build.py` against the synthetic fixture: no placeholders remain.
- No real personal data anywhere in the diff: viewer fixtures are invented people, templates hold only placeholders, `exports/` stays gitignored.

Added `.landing-*` and `.ios-*` blocks, reusing only existing tokens (no new colors). Added `.landing-brand`, `.landing-card-title`, `.ios-title` to the existing shared serif selector (not new declarations) so `designTokens.test.ts`'s "exactly 2 uses of `font-family: var(--font-serif)`" guard stays true.

- **View named `"landing"`, not `"home"`.** The brief suggested `"home"`, but that name is already load-bearing for the *authenticated* app screen in `App.tsx`. Using it for the signed-out landing would have collided. `"landing"` was already the exact term `bootMode`'s `BootMode` type uses for this concept.
- **`#/join` now resolves to `"ios"`** (not dropped, not left as `"waitlist"` since that view no longer exists) - it's kept as a public alias into the page that now carries the signup, per its own existing "must stay public" contract.

## TLDR

The site grows from one page into a small product family. The root URL now tells people what Haven is and offers the two products: Your Sky for Mac, which anyone can download and try today, and Haven for iPhone, which people can join the waitlist for. `#/sky` is the Sky landing: what it does, how the download-authorize-map flow works, exactly what stays on your Mac, and the download itself (`/downloads/YourSky.zip`, the freshly built app that renders the new acquaintance map). `#/ios` is the iPhone landing and now carries the waitlist signup that used to be the root page; `#/join` still works and lands there. Nothing about sign-in, the signed-in app, legal pages, or public cards changes.

## What changed

- `#/` (signed out): a new Haven landing in the same night-sky design language: the brand, one honest sentence about what Haven is, and two product cards. The iPhone/waitlist card sits first in DOM order so the signup path stays above the fold on a phone.
- `#/sky`: the Your Sky product page (hero, how-it-works steps, a "what stays on your Mac" privacy section whose sentences are deliberate trust boundaries, download CTAs, and the unsigned-build first-open instructions).
- `#/ios`: the iPhone product page, reusing the exact waitlist copy (still locked by its copy test) as the hero, with the extracted `WaitlistForm` component and a short "what's coming" section grounded in the MVP design doc; no invented features.
- Routing: `resolveView` gains `sky` and `ios` views, the signed-out default view is renamed `waitlist` to `landing`, and `#/join` resolves to the iOS page. Both new hashes are carved out ahead of the generic Clerk-flow check so they stay public. Signed-in visitors still resolve to their people regardless of hash.
- `WaitlistForm` keeps reporting a truthful `desktop`/`phone` source to the `joinWaitlist` mutation: extraction moved the mode decision from a container `ResizeObserver` to a window resize listener, because inside a narrow column the old approach would have permanently reported "phone". Pinned by tests at two viewport widths.
- The download artifact `public/downloads/YourSky.zip` enters the repo: the current Release build of Your Sky with the acquaintance-map viewer bundled.
- Changelog entry `v0.45.0` and matching `package.json` bump.

## Verification

- `npm test`: 41 files, 659 tests, all passing (new tests for the landing, the iOS page, the extracted form's mode reporting and states, and every new `resolveView` case, written test-first).
- `npm run build`: typecheck and production build pass; the built bundle contains the new copy and carries the download zip.
- Unrelated working-tree files (env example, skills lockfile, docs, graph tooling) verified untouched and left out of the branch.

## Flagged for a decision, deliberately not resolved here

- The constellation lens interaction (the drag gesture that revealed the figure on the old waitlist page) is now unmounted: the old page was the only caller passing `lens` into `DriftSky`. The lens code and its 24 tests remain intact and green, but no live page uses it. Re-adding it needs a placement decision (landing? iOS page? both?) plus small CSS work, since the new pages scroll and dim the sky canvas.
- `index.html`'s meta description still says "Join the private beta", which described the old root. Left alone per the no-SEO-overhaul scope; worth one line in a follow-up.
